lesson.title: Beyond Integration: The Rise of Black Power
lesson.summary: Emerging in the mid-1960s, the Black Power movement pushed past the Civil Rights Act's promise of legal equality to demand Black political and economic self-determination, cultural pride, and, for some, armed self-defense.
lesson.body:
By the mid-1960s, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 had outlawed segregation in public accommodations and discrimination in employment, a landmark legal achievement. Yet for many Black Americans, especially outside the South, daily life changed little: segregated and underfunded neighborhoods, police brutality, and persistent poverty remained largely untouched by the new law. Frustration was especially sharp in Northern and Western cities, and it boiled over into unrest, notably in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles in August 1965, just days after the Voting Rights Act had been signed.

The phrase "Black Power" entered wide public use in June 1966 during the March Against Fear, a voting rights walk through Mississippi that James Meredith, who had been the first Black student to attend the University of Mississippi, began alone before being shot and wounded. As other activists, including Stokely Carmichael, chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, continued the march, Carmichael began calling for "Black Power" rather than integration alone, signaling a shift within SNCC and elsewhere away from strict nonviolence and interracial coalition building and toward Black-led self-determination.

The movement drew heavily on ideas Malcolm X had championed before his 1965 assassination: pride in Black history and culture, skepticism that white America would grant genuine equality without sustained struggle, and the right of Black communities to defend themselves. Slogans like "Black is Beautiful" encouraged pride in natural hair and African heritage, and college campuses saw the first Black studies programs take shape.

The most visible organizational expression of Black Power was the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense, founded in Oakland, California, in October 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale. The Panthers organized armed patrols to monitor police conduct in Black neighborhoods, which drew national attention and, in turn, surveillance and repression from the FBI's COINTELPRO program. But the party's daily work centered heavily on community "survival programs," including free breakfast programs for schoolchildren and free health clinics.

Black Power was never a single organization but a broad and varied current, ranging from cultural pride and self-help to more revolutionary politics, that coexisted uneasily alongside the mainstream civil rights movement's continued legal and legislative victories. Its critique of segregated, impoverished urban neighborhoods pointed directly toward the next major legislative fight: housing discrimination.
